platforms.name: YouTube Live
platforms.rationale: YouTube asks for CBR with a 2 s keyframe interval (4 s is the hard limit). AV1 and HEVC need 30 to 40 percent less bitrate than H.264 for the same picture, so they come first; H.264 stays as the fallback every viewer path accepts. Playback is normalised to about -14 LUFS, so mixing there avoids YouTube turning the level down. AV1 cannot carry HDR; HDR needs 10-bit HEVC.
uncertain: AV1 over Enhanced RTMP ingest (YouTube documents AV1 and HEVC, but the accepted transport varies by account and rollout)
the 35000 kbps StreamStack cap (YouTube lists up to about 51000 for 4K60 H.264)

platforms.name: Twitch
platforms.rationale: Twitch wants CBR and a 2 s keyframe interval. 6000 kbps is the safe ceiling for 1080p60 on H.264 (partners may go to 8500). Enhanced Broadcasting accepts HEVC and AV1 on supported accounts, which gives the same quality at lower bitrate; the encoder falls back to H.264 when the account is not enrolled.
uncertain: HEVC and AV1 ingest depend on the account being enrolled in Enhanced Broadcasting
Twitch publishes no loudness target; -16 LUFS is a common creator choice, not a rule
8500 kbps is a partner figure from third-party guides

platforms.name: Kick
platforms.rationale: Kick ingests H.264 over RTMPS, CBR, 2 s keyframes, up to 1080p60 and about 8000 kbps. 6000 kbps leaves headroom on shared uplinks.
uncertain: no first-party Kick document was found; every figure comes from encoder vendors and guides
no loudness target is published

platforms.name: TikTok Live
platforms.rationale: TikTok Live is vertical (9:16). 1080x1920 H.264 at 30 fps and 4 to 6 Mbps is the common recommendation. RTMP access needs an eligible account and the stream key changes each session.
uncertain: TikTok publishes no ingest specification; guides disagree on 30 versus 60 fps and on bitrate
RTMP access is gated by account eligibility
no loudness target is published

platforms.name: LinkedIn Live
platforms.rationale: LinkedIn recommends 720p (1080p is the maximum) at 30 fps, 3.5 Mbps video (6 Mbps maximum), AAC 128 kbps at 48 kHz, 2 s keyframes, RTMP or RTMPS, and at least 10 Mbps of upload. It is stricter than other platforms about frame rate. If processing fails, drop to the Baseline H.264 profile to avoid B-frame timestamp issues.
uncertain: the official table is written for cloud-service ingest; a direct encoder connection may behave differently
StreamStack caps at 4500 kbps, between the recommended 3500 and the 6000 maximum

platforms.name: Facebook Live
platforms.rationale: Facebook Live takes H.264 and AAC only, CBR, a 2 s keyframe interval (4 s maximum), 1080p at 30 fps and 3 to 6 Mbps. Its own encoder-configuration API example uses 1080p30 at 6000 kbps with a 60-frame GOP.
uncertain: some guides claim 1080p60 and up to 15000 kbps; Facebook's own example is 1080p30 at 6000 kbps, which is what this preset follows
no loudness target is published

platforms.name: X Live
platforms.rationale: X Live Studio (which replaced Media Studio Producer) recommends H.264 at 1080p60 and 12 Mbps, up to 4K60 and 40 Mbps, AAC 128 kbps, Main or High profile and a keyframe every 3 s.
uncertain: only one search result described the new Live Studio figures; older Producer guidance (9 Mbps, 720p60) still circulates
StreamStack stops at 1080p60 although X allows 4K60

platforms.name: Teams, Zoom and Meet camera
platforms.rationale: Calling apps encode the camera themselves, so StreamStack hands them raw frames through the virtual camera and the microphone through the virtual source. 720p30 is what every app handles on a weak link and 1080p30 is the useful maximum; none of them benefit from 60 fps.
uncertain: each app picks its own resolution from its bandwidth estimate; this preset only sets what StreamStack offers
no loudness target applies, the apps run their own gain control

platforms.name: Local archive
platforms.rationale: A recording is not limited by an uplink, so it uses constant quality (not a bitrate) with the most efficient codec the hardware has. Matroska survives a crash or power cut with a playable file, and holds Opus. The audio is not loudness-normalised so the editor keeps the full range.
uncertain: the quality numbers are starting points for VA-API global_quality and need tuning against the real Arc encoder

platforms.name: Self-hosted relay (SRT or WHIP)
platforms.rationale: For a relay you run (MediaMTX, a CDN contribution link, a remote production). SRT carries AV1, HEVC and Opus with low latency, and WHIP carries H.264 and Opus (HEVC and AV1 when the server accepts them); the 1 s keyframe interval keeps joins and recovery fast. Tune the SRT latency to about four times the round-trip time.
uncertain: not a published platform, the numbers are StreamStack's own defaults
WHIP needs the streamstack[whip] extra and a server that accepts the codec; H.264 is the safe choice
